items.title: The Red Queen hypothesis – a new way forward for self-improving AI
items.story_key: story|title:the red queen hypothesis a new way forward for self improving ai
items.content_excerpt: The research team, which includes collaborators from NVIDIA and Flower Labs, have come up with a new method for recursive self-improving AI agents to continue improving themselves (by repeatedly testing and enhancing their own code) without hitting the evaluation ceiling that they frequently encounter. Their method also suggests a way of cutting the costs of the computational resource needed for the development of such AI agents. While agents can already improve themselves by editing their own code, testing variants, and keeping changes that perform better, this process is usually limited by a fixed evaluator, benchmark, or test suite. Once the agent has learned everything that fixed signal can distinguish, improvement slows or stalls. "A self-improving agent can only get as good as the test that scores it," explains team member Alex Iacob , a PhD student in the Machine Learning Systems Lab under the supervision of Prof Nic Lane . "The test does not merely measure progress, it defines it, so the efficacy of the test becomes a ceiling the agent cannot climb past." Now the researchers have addressed this issue by having both the self-improving agent and the evaluator evolve together. "Instead of improving an agent against a fixed test, we let the evaluation evolve alongside the agent ," Alex adds. "As the agent gets better, the evaluation also gets harder , and the bar keeps rising." Alex is the first author on the pre-print paper the research team has just uploaded to arXiv. The Red Queen Gödel Machine: Co-Evolving Agents and Their Evaluators shares the technical details of their work, along with some impressive results from using this framework across a number of tasks. Figure: Agents and evaluators improving together. The Red Queen Gödel Machine searches through many possible versions of an AI agent, while also improving the evaluator that judges those agents. During each phase, the evaluator is kept fixed so progress can be measured reliably. At checkpoints, a stronger evaluator can replace the old one if it performs better on trusted ground-truth examples. Scores from the old evaluator are then removed, so the next phase is guided by the new, more demanding standard. This creates a self-improving loop in which agents and evaluators improve together, while the system remains anchored to reliable checks. items.title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
items.summary:
Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven't unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping. The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn't want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator, a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room.

Here's what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while:

You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners - I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra.

The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn't work particularly well, so I added a "Rough mode" where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds.

Once that's set up, the devices all listen for the beep!

I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room - displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound.

Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the "Sounds located" log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click "This is the mystery beep" to mark them as such.

Once you've confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map.

The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced.

How it works

When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices, a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here's that paper's abstract:

We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting.

That sounded exactly like what we needed to build!

Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see detector.js), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server.

When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep.

How I built it

I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here's that shared starter session, which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository:

Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solve

There is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find it

I want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes from

There needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server app

Ideally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though?

That got me this problem.md file. As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file.

The research looked good, so I told it:

Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something else

That got me to this point - most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet.

I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then Fable 5.2 was released, and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces.

I had Claude Code on my laptop start the server running, then made sure it could both see what was happening and make live changes to the software as it ran.

This was already baked into the software: Opus 5.5 had built an installModule() method on the listeners that could be triggered over the WebSocket connection, meaning the admin server could execute arbitrary new code on any of its clients.

On some devices, web pages that listen on the microphone request user permission any time the page reloads. The hot-swap module mechanism meant that we could deploy new code without having to manually interact with each of the listening devices in turn.

From that point on my involvement was mainly to sit by the laptop chatting with Fable 5.2 about what was going on, and occasionally requesting new features. Here are some of the feature prompts I ran:

I think we need to make it so I can drag things around on the map in “rough mode”, where my job is just to put them roughly where they are, then switch out of rough mode and it attempts to get them accurate

This gave me the ability to drag listeners around the map.

what’s a good way for me to test this I wonder? Can we have it listen for claps, then I could clap and it could identify the location of the clap? [...]

Claps should use a different symbol on the map than beeps

That added the thing where any time I clapped it would show on the map as a different symbol from the beeps.

each symbol on the map should include a HH:MM:SS timestamp

That made it easier to spot which symbol likely reflected which real-world sound.

The log should show beeps and claps with their timestamps AND have a little play button which, when clicked, replays the recorded noise from each of the listeners in sequence (with clear text on screen showing which listener recorded which snippet) while temporarily turning off microphone recording while that replay plays

Now I could replay sounds, making it much easier to identify which recorded clip was the mysterious beep I was looking for.

There should be a button next to a recording for “This is the mystery beep” - then I can hit replay to see and then confirm it was the mystery beep if that’s the one I am looking for

Then the system can categorize noises in the future to see if they are likely that same mysterious beep and use that information to build a more accurate idea of where it is

At this point I was getting close - I had a solid idea of where the beep was coming from, but wouldn't it be neat if I could reposition the listeners around that point to get an even finer location?

I want a feature for this, I don’t want to have to restart each listening device etc, I want to be able to click a “Reposition the devices” button which lets me switch into repositioning, then I click “Repositioned” and it puts me into Rough mode and asks me to roughly locate them, then I do that and click, then it starts up again. The previous session can be read-only viewed through the app.

And since I had one spare device, I then said:

add a feature where the map includes a spot that is a suggestion for a location that it would be useful to add a listener at - based on data collected so far

Giving Claude Code ears

I think the most interesting part of this project is that I demonstrated it's possible to give Claude Code ears.

Claude doesn't have native audio input (yet), but it can run JavaScript and Python code that can analyze audio captured by a microphone.

I told it to run a web server with WebSocket connections to multiple listening devices, then had it both run a WebAudio microphone on those devices and hook them up so they could be sent fresh JavaScript code to execute via that WebSocket.

Then I could pretty much leave Claude alone, hacking away at the problem, querying the audio logs, and reconfiguring its ears to help it solve the problem.

I'm reminded of a similar hack I heard about at GitHub Universe a few weeks ago, where Martin Woodward told me he had been debugging the GitHub Universe Badge computers by plugging them into a computer via USB-C and then pointing a webcam at their screen, so his coding agent could tell if updates were working correctly or not.

Figuring out ways to let coding agents perceive the world around them is a whole lot of fun.

items.title: Show HN: ZTHR – what replaces code review when AI agents write all the code
items.story_key: story|title:zthr what replaces code review when ai agents write all the code
items.content_excerpt: ZTHR is a pattern language for software built by AI. Nothing is trusted because it says so, and quality comes from the environment the author works in, not from the author. Every part of the example on one page: the app, its admin, the evidence, the docs and the case. A reference app built entirely by agents under ZTHR fixtures: what it does and who it is for. Gates, walks, every test, mutation, the sensitive-data trace and the block library. Generating code is now nearly free. Deciding whether it is right is not. So stop asking people to read every diff, and build a factory that cannot be fooled: governed parts that limit what can be built, checks proven to fail on the defects they exist to catch, and statements of user intent the author cannot rewrite. Let the models try as many times as it takes. Ship only what passes. Turn every miss into a new check. No author, reviewer, model, operator or report gains authority by asserting success. A claim counts only on evidence the claimant does not control. Quality moves out of the author's skill and into the environment. Generators iterate until the fixtures are satisfied. Little, R. (2026). ZTHR: A Pattern Language for Autonomous Software Delivery (Version 1.0). Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23826734 You have a robot that can build a thousand bookshelves a day. It is fast, it is getting smarter, and it always says it did a great job. You could check every shelf by hand. You would never keep up, and by the five-hundredth shelf you would miss things. This is code review when AI writes the code: the reviewer becomes the bottleneck or a rubber stamp. So you build a jig : a frame that holds the wood so the shelf can only go together one way. In software: a shared foundation and a catalog of tested parts, so the robot does not reinvent the locks and hinges every time. Then you build a gauge : a tester that tries every shelf and says fits or does not fit. And you test the tester. You hand it a broken shelf on purpose and make sure it says no. You do not only check each board. You check what people want: can you put books on it? Now the robot can try as many times as it needs. Bad shelves go back. Only shelves that pass every test leave the factory. When a bad shelf ever slips through, you do not only fix that shelf. You build a new test so that kind of mistake can never slip through again. Nobody is believed just because they say it worked. Not the robot, not the tester, not the boss. Russ Little · v1.0 · © 2

items.content_excerpt: Self-hosted voice AI agents with a Vapi-compatible API. AI phone agents on Twilio, Telnyx, Plivo, Vonage or SIP, with your keys or 100% local and free (Whisper, Ollama, Kokoro). No per-minute platform fee. npx openring The open-source, self-hosted Vapi alternative for voice AI agents. Vapi-compatible API, no platform fee. OpenRing runs AI phone agents, voice AI agents and AI receptionists that answer and place calls over Twilio, Telnyx, Plivo, Vonage or any SIP trunk, with your own provider keys or a free, 100% local stack (Whisper, Ollama, Kokoro). Quick start · How it works · Compare · API guide · Providers · Roadmap · Discussions Hosted voice platforms charge a fee for every minute of every call, on top of what you already pay for speech-to-text, the model, the voice and the phone line. OpenRing does the same job on your own computer or server, with your own provider keys, and speaks the same JSON as Vapi. You need Node.js 18 or later. Everything else, Python included, installs itself: Settings live in ~/.openring/.env , created on the first run with a generated API key for apps that call the API (it's under Settings ). The free Kokoro voice downloads itself on the first start (about 120 MB). Each call runs a Pipecat pipeline: the caller's speech becomes text, the model answers (and can call your tools), and the voice speaks the answer back. Every turn's latency is recorded, step by step, and shown in the dashboard. — means we didn't find it in their public docs. On every platform you also pay for the model, the voice and the phone line, and for speech-to-text too, except that Retell's pricing page lists no separate charge for it. With OpenRing, the server, its uptime and any compliance work are yours; hosted platforms take on the first two and help with the third (for HIPAA, Vapi charges US$2,000 a month and Retell says there's no extra fee). Prices and features are from each company's public pages and docs on November 8, 2026 (prices rechecked that day); check them before you decide. OpenRing isn't affiliated with any of them. Copy every assistant, squad, tool and Twilio number of an account in one request, or press Import on the Assistants page. The key is used once and never stored; importing again updates what came in before. The answer lists each assistant with anything that keeps it from taking calls here yet (for example a provider OpenRing doesn't support yet). Documents keep their full JSON, so nothing is lost. items.title: What Is Eval-Driven Development? How to Improve AI Agents
items.summary: Eval-driven development helps you build AI agents against a consistent set of metrics. Define good behavior, write the eval first, then compare experiments.
items.story_key: story|title:what is eval driven development how to improve ai agents
items.content_excerpt: Development on most agents starts the same way. You write a prompt, try a few questions by hand, adjust, and try again. This works well in the beginning, when agent errors are obvious and improvements are easy to see. But over time it becomes increasingly difficult to know whether your most recent change made an agent better or worse. Eval-driven development (EDD) solves this by giving you a consistent set of metrics to measure your agent’s performance against and guide your decision making. Here at LangChain we've used EDD when building our most advanced agents (check out our blog on IssueBench ), and have boiled it down to a three step process: In this blog, we'll walk through this process step by step so that your team can apply it to your own agent development process. The name and concept of eval-driven development borrows from test-driven development (TDD), where you write a failing test before writing the code that passes it. Agents differ from traditional code as they're non-deterministic: As a result, agents need a different kind of test. An eval handles this by scoring runs of your agent across a set of examples. Evals are more flexible than traditional testing. You can score any aspect of the agent's run and you can use other LLMs to score it ( LLM-as-a-judge ). With EDD, similar to TDD, these evals become your definition of success and you build your agent towards them. The first step in EDD is defining what your agent should do. Then, list the behaviors it needs to handle to get there. These could be tasks such as answering questions from a knowledge base, taking an action on a user's behalf, or knowing when to ask a follow-up question. Write down the requirements for each behavior. Together, these make up a product requirements document (PRD) for your agent. EDD works on one behavior at a time. This gives you a narrow target to hill climb toward, without one change muddying the effect of another. The behavior you pick usually comes from a feature you're about to build or a failure you found in your agent's past runs. Before writing code, it’s helpful to define a short spec that covers: Say we have an internal docs agent that employees query for company information. It has two tools: search_docs for internal documentation and web_search for everything else. We plan to add a create_ticket tool so it can file IT tickets. items.title: Agent Self-Improvement with Frozen Weights: The Added Value and Limits of Failure Traces
items.summary: We evaluate whether an AI agent's harness, the notes around its model, can learn from the agent's failure traces beyond a matched search that never sees them. It can, but less than it looks. We tested an open 9-billion-parameter model with fixed weights; a larger teacher model wrote its notes. On generated customer-service decisions, where both note writers were told the target rules, notes based on the agent's mistakes improved accuracy by 4.0 percentage points over notes from the same process with the mistakes withheld. That process alone, trying and keeping better-scoring notes, reached about 60% of the total improvement. In full customer-service conversations the same notes showed no demonstrated improvement. Separately, a strict screen of single lessons admitted two customer-service lessons, still awaiting tests on new data, and one tool-use lesson, written without seeing the agent's mistakes, which showed no demonstrated gain on new tool-use tasks. A neutral note with no procedure scored higher than the learned lessons (exploratory). A blind audit judged 146 of 240 tool-use test items defective.

items.title: ScrapeBench: Evaluating Legal Compliance of AI Agents in Website Scraping
items.summary: AI agents deployed on the open web are becoming more capable of performing actions that may breach contractual provisions and violate computer security laws. In this paper, we introduce ScrapeBench, the first agentic benchmark for empirically evaluating the legal compliance of AI agents with website scraping policies, namely terms of service (ToS) and robots.txt directives. Across widely used closed-weight and open-weight AI agents, we find that most agents exhibit low compliance rates (< 5%) when instructed to scrape websites in our sample of 1,626 popular websites that explicitly prohibit scraping. In addition, we observe that even where AI agents actively check the applicable ToS and robots.txt, they continue to exhibit low compliance rates. Conversely, in our sample of 269 websites that do not prohibit scraping, we observe that agents sometimes refuse to scrape despite it being lawful, such as Claude Opus 4.6 exhibiting an over-refusal rate of 98.5%. Our human baseline experiments (n = 180 participants) suggest that humans exhibit compliance rates comparable to AI agents but over-refuse at much higher rates.

items.title: Release 2.74.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.10
items.summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • The S3 addressing style is now configurable.
  • Request cancellation is now checked before a request is dispatched to the backend, and before batch assembly in the TensorRT backend.
  • Tutorials: The Llava1.5 guide is deprecated in favor of the new Qwen2.5-VL guide for the TensorRT-LLM PyTorch backend. Note: this is a breaking change.
  • HTTP request buffers are now released after a request is rejected for exceeding the chunk limit.
  • --http-max-input-size is now enforced across nested parameters of generate requests.
  • SageMaker model URLs are now validated before path normalization.
  • Fixed copying of the cuBLAS libraries to the CUDA targets lib directory.
  • Relaxed the openai and pydantic pins to match vLLM requirements.
  • Tritonserver is now built on, and shipped on, the cuda-dl-base devel image.
  • Python backend: Restrictive permissions are now applied to shared memory, and GPU tensor allocation now falls back to host memory.
  • ONNX Runtime, OpenVINO, Python and TensorRT-LLM backends: Backend builds now require TRITON_BUILD_CONTAINER instead of synthesizing a py3-min image.
  • vLLM backend: Added support for vLLM >= 0.30, and prompts are now rendered before generation and encoding.
  • Triton CLI: The image fetch in the TRT-LLM preprocessing template is now bounded.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.

items.title: D-REAL: Acceptance-Length Optimization with Unbiased Gradients for Speculative Decoding
items.summary: Speculative decoding efficiency depends on the number of consecutively accepted draft tokens, yet token-level training objectives do not directly optimize this quantity. We introduce D-REAL (Drafter Reinforcement of Expected Acceptance Length), a post-training method that directly optimizes expected acceptance length for a fixed decoding context. D-REAL weights position-wise draft-target distributional overlap by prefix survival probabilities along a draft-sampled prefix, faithfully capturing the sequential dependence of verification on earlier proposals. By accounting for the parameter dependence of the proposal distribution, we derive an unbiased gradient estimator for this single-round objective under stochastic verification. We evaluate D-REAL on DSpark and DFlash2 with Qwen3-8B as the target model across ten benchmarks. Starting from baselines whose mean acceptance length has plateaued, one epoch of D-REAL post-training consistently improves the benchmark-averaged mean acceptance length by up to 0.23 tokens across both architectures under greedy (T = 0.0) and stochastic (T = 1.0) sampling, translating into up to a 9.4% end-to-end serving throughput improvement.

items.title: TurnFlow: Benchmarking User-State Reasoning in Multi-Turn LLM Agents via Scene-Guided User Simulation
items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed through conversational interfaces, yet strong single-turn performance does not imply reliability in multi-turn settings. Multi-turn assistance requires a model to maintain an evolving representation of user requirements and to reason over it before complying with later requests. Failures can therefore be subtle: models may fail to recognize a changed constraint or hidden conflict, or recognize it without enforcing it in the final response. Existing benchmarks primarily test fully specified prompts, long-context recall, or controlled domain environments, leaving open-domain requirement reconciliation undermeasured. We introduce TurnFlow, an interactive benchmark for evaluating whether models preserve, revise, and act on user requirements across turns. TurnFlow combines adaptive user simulation with verifiable judging, allowing conversations to unfold naturally while keeping hidden requirements and pass/fail criteria controlled. In our evaluation, nine LLMs achieve overall pass rates from 42.86% to 59.59% on 490 scenarios. Performance varies substantially across challenge types: models perform well on Stateful Multi-Constraint Following but remain considerably less reliable on Scope Creep and Goal Shift. These results reveal persistent limitations in reasoning over evolving user requirements across turns.

What happens when students can one-shot last year’s homework? Inside CS146S and the engineering team at Monaco. The AI Engineer YouTube channel just crossed one million subscribers . Thank you to everyone who’s watched a talk, sent one to a teammate, or put something they learned into production. For this special, we wanted to sit down with someone who has to answer a question a lot of us are asking at work: what should a software engineer actually learn now? Mihail Eric has two places to test his answer. He teaches The Modern Software Developer at Stanford and leads AI at Monaco, where his colleagues use coding agents to ship software and investigate outages. I asked him to take us through the syllabus, then tell us which parts survived contact with his own engineering team. This is also meant as a preview for all of you joining us in San Francisco for AIE Code next week, as required knowledge for all the conversations with the speakers, sponsors and attendees you’re about to have. If you can see this as a LS subscriber and haven’t got a ticket yet, you can use this code for 30% off (no refunds, sorry) The first run of CS146S had nine assignments and a capstone. In one exercise, students ran an AI code reviewer on a repo and evaluated its feedback. By the next run, Mihail figured students could one-shot a lot of those exercises. When he asked a room of Stanford sophomores and juniors how they coded, everyone he surveyed was already using an agent. So this time, part of the homework is contributing to an open-source project. The person who maintains the repo reviews the student’s patch. I like what that does to the assignment. You can ask an agent to implement a feature in an afternoon. You still have to find out whether the maintainer wants it, why the code behaves the way it does, and what else your patch might break. That conversation is also how a junior engineer gets to learn from a senior one. There’s an exercise in the episode you can borrow for your next PR. items.title: The Iron(wood) Throne: Google's TPU Stakes Its Claim on Inference
items.summary: Viable Alternative of CUDA Moat, NVIDIA scared and working nights & weekends, Jensen’s Counter Submission, Kimi K3, Muse Spark Open, Qwen, GLM5.3, TorchTPU, vLLM, SGLang, llm-d, Ray
items.story_key: story|title:the iron wood throne google s tpu stakes its claim on inference
items.content_excerpt: In November 2025, we published a newsletter saying that Google is selling TPUs to external customers. Since then, we have been proven right over and over again with Oracle, OpenAI , Anthropic, and Meta all becoming customers of TPUs just as our Accelerator Model reported. Hardware demand is only half the story, as NVIDIA’s moat has historically been its software and large developer ecosystem. This is where TPU is also making headway, partnering with upstream maintainers across the entire ecosystem, including the Meta PyTorch team, vLLM (Inferact, RedHat), SGLang (RadixArk), llm-d, Ray, etc. This is not a surprise to folks that have read our September 2026 article laying out Google TPU’s externalization strategy . Back in our September article, we published the first third-party TPUv7 results on InferenceX on single-turn workloads, showing that in an apples-to-apples FP8 comparison on Qwen 3.5 397B, TPUv7 Ironwood) delivered up to 50% better performance per dollar than B200 and B300. We also reported that many Google TPU customers were asking for AgentX results, since long-context, multi-turn agentic serving is where inference spend is heading. Previously, Jensen went on the Dwarkesh Podcast and commented on the fact that no other chips were taking advantage of their opportunity to show performance on InferenceX. Six months later, and indeed Google is taking full advantage of this opportunity. Today we are releasing the first official long-context, multi-turn, realistic agentic inference benchmark results on TPUv7 across four models, showing that TPUv7 is either competitive on perf per dollar for external customers or delivers the best state-of-the-art result: Muse Spark Open SGLang AgentX (NVFP4 weights): Competitive TPU performance per dollar result even though the architecture was co-designed for GPUs. Submitted by OSS ecosystem developer, RadixArk (Makers of SGLang). GLM-5.2 vLLM AgentX (FP8): TPUv7 is the cheapest FP8 option, delivering 1.2x to 2.7x the tokens per dollar of B200, B300, and MI355X from 60 to 300 tok/s/user. NVIDIA NVFP4 still beats TPUv7 FP8, but with accuracy / quality loss. Qwen3.5 vLLM AgentX (FP8): With llm-d disaggregated serving, TPUv7 beats GB300 FP8 at every interactivity level and restores parity even against GB300 FP4 at higher quality / accuracy. Kimi K3 vLLM AgentX (MXFP4 weights): Competitive with GB300 NVL72 at launch; With TPUv7 delivering 1.15x to 2.5x the tokens per dollar of GB200, B200, B300, and MI355X. Submitted by
